video: Hardin Jefferson ISD ver26 sub
cleaned_text: Fritz Deckard exemplifies an unwavering commitment to advancing his district while setting a standard for leadership and innovation. Before, we had a single AC unit for the classrooms, which caused every issue you could imagine: humidity, airflow, and fresh air problems, all because we had only one thermostat. E3 came in with a team that helped us present this to the board so we could get the money allocated to move the project forward. The energy savings from a project like this are huge. School districts are always looking for areas where they can save and reallocate funds to the classrooms. Anything you can do to be more efficient keeps money where it belongs—in the classroom with teachers and students. We went from an energy usage rating of about 138 on the scale to sub-30s now. We are projected to be at about 28 to 31 depending on usage for the summer. When you start to talk about that, most newer buildings hope to hit 35, so it is a dramatic difference. A big part of the benefit is that I no longer hear teachers talking about being uncomfortable in their classrooms. The lighting is softer on the eyes and easier on the children; it is an overall improvement that everyone has gotten comfortable with, and we no longer hear those complaints. All of our educational pods now have their own thermostats for control. The lighting exchange performed by E3 was night and day, literally. We went from being dark as a dungeon to a bright space where the colors on the walls really stand out. The trustworthiness of the E3 staff, their workers, and their overall communication is outstanding. E3 communicates very well. I am a big relationship guy, and I believe it is important to have a high level of trust. I have that high level of trust with E3. They really showed up, took a step back to look at the building in its entirety, and committed to putting it back exactly the way they found it, if not better. That is not like normal contractors today, where you often hear, 'That's not my job,' if a floor gets scratched. E3 took the time to show they valued our trust, and they earned it.

video: Highland Park ISD - Central plant upgrades
cleaned_text: We are currently contracting with E3 and DMI to replace the hydronic piping in our central plant at Highland Park Middle School, taking care of the chiller piping and condenser water piping from top to bottom.

video: Lake Worth, case study
cleaned_text: As we create a learning environment for the children of Lake Worth, we take everything into consideration, whether it's the curriculum, hiring the very best teachers for the classroom, the quality of the lighting, or the temperature. We want to ensure our kids are in a comfortable learning situation. Our concern was replacing the HVAC units, but we also had to assess our financials because we want to be good stewards of the taxpayers' money. There were several places we could save money, so we needed to move forward and get a long-range plan in place. The night that E3 did presentations to the school board, there were a lot of questions, and they were handled very well. When that evening was over, the board had a very good understanding of where we were going and why we were going there. With the support E3 provided for us, I think we made some wise financial decisions. The lighting E3 replaced for us has already created a better learning environment. One of our gyms is probably 60 years old, and the lighting in there is now much more inviting to our students, plus we are saving money because it is much more efficient. The exterior lighting has been huge. Some of our schools open early in the morning, sometimes before the sun is up, and I think the improved lighting brings security to the teachers and staff members who enter in the mornings. Lastly, we appreciate knowing that we can call E3 for support later on and that you are going to be there for us.

video: Learning opportunity for students.mp4
cleaned_text: It was very exciting that our fifth graders were doing some studies in science about saving energy and conserving. They did some research as young elementary students and came up with the idea that we could apply for a SECO grant and get funding for an LED project. Little did they know, we were already thinking about it and talking about it. So, it was really fun to bring them together, bring TASB and E3 to the table, and let everyone talk about saving energy with the lighting project. Right now, Caldwell has been approved, and we are about to take on that project. Now that these kids are sixth graders, we are excited that E3 is going to come back and talk to them about energy conservation as well. We are able to save the taxpayers money and improve lighting for our schools, and our kids are all part of learning about the importance of taking care of their environment.

video: Lessons In Learning - Judd Marshall, Superintendent,  Mount Pleasant ISD
cleaned_text: I think kids come from a lot of different environments. The nuclear family is not what it once was; it has a very different look now. They bring a unique set of issues, concerns, and values to our classrooms. Sometimes those things contribute to learning, so it is not all bad or all good—it is just different. We have had to learn to adapt because we have to do things for kids now that I did not have to do 29 years ago when I started. We can either adjust and meet them at the door the way they come to us, or we are going to fail. I remember when I was in college, I was mowing my great-grandmother's yard. It was hot, I was tired, and she asked me what was wrong. I said, 'Mama, I'm just not ready to go back to college. It's hot, and I just don't want to go back.' She said, 'Let me tell you something: education is something that no one can ever take from you. I have a sixth-grade education, and you don't want to do what I had to do to make a living. You go back to school, get your degree, and make the world a better place.' That changed my attitude, and I went back to college and finished. I say all that to say this: no paycheck beats watching those kids walk across the stage on graduation night—especially the ones where, when they were freshmen, you thought there was no way in the world they would finish. It brings tears to your eyes because you know you had a small part in the success they achieved. The Pride Pathway program, which is a partnership we have with A&M-Commerce, allows us to continue to 'grow our own.' We have staff working in our district who do not have college degrees, and the Pride Pathway program helps them earn one. We hired someone recently who brought tears to my eyes because they never thought they would make the kind of money they are making as a first-year teacher at Mount Pleasant ISD. They were one of those kids where you thought there was no way they would make it across the stage, but they did. They made something of themselves, and I am really proud of that. That is what makes it all worth it.

video: Lessons In Learning - Mike Lamb, Superintendent, Little Elm ISD
cleaned_text: I would say I'm competitive. That drive to win makes you want to do well. What makes me competitive? Strangely enough, I think my math skills and analytical ability have helped me a lot in leadership. If I were to ask anyone what they did not like about math, what do you guess most people would say? For many, the hardest part of math is reading the word problem and sticking with it. I would draw pictures—that was competitive to me. I was good at math because I was competitive and did not want the page to beat me. As a young child, I think a lot of people would say I wasn't very competitive because I lost a lot. At some point, I just wanted to play; I didn't really care if I won or lost, I just wanted to participate without arguing or fighting. Most of the time, particularly when I was young, that meant I got beat a lot. I remember playing with my big brother on the trampoline; he would beat me at everything we did. But playing with those older kids paid off later on, helping me develop the ability to finally start winning. Those hard times helped push me through. Being competitive and learning how to win eventually led to a football scholarship and the ability to earn a math degree, so it all circles back and ties together. You cannot be afraid to fail; you learn so much from failure and from trying over and over. Think about all the great inventors and how many iterations they went through. We had gotten to a point in education where we thought we had to have the right answer quickly or things weren't good. Now, we are starting to realize that we have to create some uncomfortable scenarios where students learn as much from failure as they do from success. After I graduated from Commerce, I went to work in Lindale for eight years, then McKinney, Huntsville, and Forney. During those times, I was never very close to Commerce—close enough to feel connected, but not active. I remember when I got the Sulphur Springs job, which is only fifteen minutes from Commerce, I told myself I wanted to get involved and help the university that helped me so much. Living close to Commerce, it didn't take long before I was asked to serve as president of the A&M-Commerce Alumni Association. It has been incredibly rewarding to get involved, give back, and help other students have the same great experience I had by supporting scholarship development for those who might not otherwise be able to afford it.

video: Lessons In Learning - Shannon Trejo, Deputy Commissioner of Schools Programs, Texas Education Agency
cleaned_text: I have a mantra, an idea that I live by, that I believe in, and that I have instilled in my own children, the children I have taught, and the leaders I have worked with throughout my career. My mantra is 'Aut viam inveniam aut faciam,' which is a Latin phrase that means, 'I will find a way or I will make one.' I grew up in Pasadena, Texas, a suburb of Houston, and was fortunate to be in a family with plenty of resources, great parents, and a great school district. I didn't really understand that there were many kids out there who didn't have those same opportunities. When I graduated from high school, I thought I knew what my career would be, coming from a background in business and real estate. However, I started tutoring at an elementary school in South Austin. Almost immediately after the kids sat down and we opened our books to read, the teacher came over and moved three children off to a corner. Everyone, including myself, watched them go, wondering what was happening. Afterward, I asked the teacher what happened and what I could do differently to include them. She replied, 'Oh, no, they don't speak English, so they're going to be placed in special education.' I started asking questions about how they learn English and realized I wanted to do something about it. Since I didn't speak Spanish, I knew I needed to learn. I moved abroad, lived overseas, and learned Spanish, experiencing what it is like to assimilate into a completely different culture. I learned to appreciate different cultures and gained a deeper appreciation for what we have in the United States. When I came back, I started my career as a third-grade bilingual teacher. Everyone wants to be told they are capable. Everyone wants to be told they are smart and can succeed. That is where my mantra comes from; it is never a question of if you can or cannot, but how hard you are willing to work to get there and how resilient you will be in overcoming the barriers in your way. Texas A&M University-Commerce was a natural choice for me when seeking my superintendent certificate. One of the things I truly appreciated was having Dr. Parra lead the program because I acknowledged to him early on what my programmatic weaknesses were. After 30 years of experience in the school system, I know what I do well, but I was not as strong in school finance, budgeting, and numbers. At a superintendent level, a high-level understanding isn't enough; you must truly understand how the numbers work to guide a district, stay out of financial trouble, and manage contracts and bond systems. Sometimes it's about confidence, but mostly it's about truly knowing your stuff. The superintendency certificate program at A&M-Commerce was highly hands-on and experiential. We attended board meetings, met with mentor superintendents, and walked through real-world scenarios. You leave feeling as though you could step right into the superintendent's chair, navigate those community and board relationships, and stay focused on what really matters: the students.

video: Lessons in Learning - Dr. Theresa Williams, Superintendent, Plano ISD
cleaned_text: Learning to be comfortable with the uncomfortable is pretty much the norm in leadership. I have run several marathons and half-marathons; as you train, you are sore and your muscles ache, but then you are able to accomplish your goal. Leadership is very similar. You set new goals, work incredibly hard—even when it is tiring and exhausting—and you achieve them. But once you finish, you immediately ask, 'What can we do better? What is the next race?' That is what it means to be comfortable with the uncomfortable. It is also what keeps me going personally: the drive to do it again, but do it better the next year. I was recently asked what I would tell my 25-year-old self, and my response was that I would actually want to know what my 25-year-old self would tell me now. There is so much wisdom in our young people. Whenever I meet with my superintendent's student advisory, I leave inspired by their feedback. We often underestimate the potential and power that our youth have to share. Growing up, elementary and middle school were safe, fun, and wonderful experiences for me. But when my family moved from a small town to a larger city, high school became very difficult. As the new student, school no longer felt safe or welcoming, and it would have been easy to fall through the cracks. In fact, I was falling through the cracks when my agriculture teacher pulled me aside one day and said, 'I'm worried about you. Just because you failed a class or a test doesn't mean you can't turn it around. Each day is a new day to be successful.' I truly believe, both as a superintendent and a mother, that kids need a place where they belong. Whether it is in clubs, sports, with a favorite teacher, or in a favorite subject, we must create those safe spaces for both our students and our employees. You often hear that it is lonely at the top, and it truly can be. As a superintendent, you are the only person with those specific duties and responsibilities. That is why building a strong network is incredibly important. I have close friends in the same role, and being able to pick up the phone and check in on shared challenges is vital. Looking back at my time at A&M-Commerce, that is where I met many of my professional colleagues. I have known other educators who went through doctoral programs without a cohort experience, and I think having Dr. Parra and going through that intensive two- to three-year journey with a group of supportive, encouraging peers was a true blessing. I am very fortunate to have met the people I did along the way.

video: Lone Star loan through SECO
cleaned_text: When we began looking at a district-wide energy efficiency design project, we considered whether to fund it out of capital or utilize a performance contract. We were leaning toward a performance contract initially, but after discussions with board members in committee meetings, we were tasked with exploring other options. The concept of shared savings was not an avenue our school board wanted to pursue. This led us to the State Energy Conservation Office (SECO) and their Lone Star program. That path was one everyone could get behind, offering a very low interest rate and allowing the district to keep all the savings rather than sharing them. There was some initial hesitation about how we would procure the project, but once we identified the right project and procurement method through the Lone Star loan with SECO, we decided to move forward with it.

video: Nano Gas - Stockdale TX Case Study, Part 1
cleaned_text: What we are currently looking at here are the wastewater treatment lagoons in Stockdale, Texas. There is a series of three lagoons where influent water enters at the head of the first pond. The issue Stockdale faces is that these ponds have never been dredged; in fact, a sonar analysis revealed that the sludge in pond number one is in excess of five feet. That is a lot of sludge. Nano Gas will be treating these ponds with our nanobubble technology and bacteria to significantly reduce the sludge in pond number one, and hopefully in ponds two and three as well, thereby increasing the efficiency of the treatment facility. This is very exciting because it gives us one of our first opportunities to showcase our technology in a lagoon with severe sludge accumulation. If we can reduce that sludge by 50% to 85%, which is our goal, it will be a huge win for Nano Gas.

video: Nano Gas - Stockdale TX Case Study, Part 2
person_name: Nano Gas - Stockdale TX Case Study Part 2 Speaker
cleaned_text: Day two of our lagoon restoration project involved taking samples from lagoon number two at the Stockdale facility. We collected 18 sludge samples, which were combined into two composite samples and submitted for analysis at the Eurofins lab in San Antonio. The sludge goes through a number of different tests. Out of curiosity, they are checking for heavy metals, which is unlikely since the influent water comes from a residential community. More importantly, we are acutely interested in whether the sludge is organic—meaning it can be digested by bacteria—or inorganic, such as silt and sand. That ratio will give us very valuable data to define the goals for this project.

They handled the design and ensured everything was installed correctly, which we really liked and knew our board would appreciate. It was easy to recommend them because they had already presented to the board, making the board comfortable with them and ensuring a very smooth process.

cleaned_text: The project successfully recycled 832 total fixtures, replacing 1,696 lamps and 785 ballasts, and installed 114 occupancy sensors, updating a total of 466 fixtures or areas.

video: Port Neches-Groves ISD, case study
cleaned_text: A year ago, we completed a $140 million bond program to build four new elementary schools in our district. That process was extremely difficult, so we were hesitant to enter into another project that might create similar challenges for the school district.

video: Port Neches-Groves ISD, case study
cleaned_text: With so many different parties involved in projects, if a problem arose, people would typically point fingers at one another. Working with E3 was a tremendous advantage because there was never a lack of communication. In a world like ours, communication is key. E3 was highly aware that we would be the ones handling maintenance when it was all said and done, and the process was incredibly smooth. Having been with the school district for 15 years, I have seen projects go well and others go poorly. This project was probably the best-run project I have ever been a part of. The new lighting is so bright it looks like a football field. When neighboring schools visit, we want to show off our facilities. E3 helped us get there, and that says a lot.

video: San Jacinto Community College, case study
cleaned_text: Before E3 came along, the biggest issues we faced were simply really old fixtures. A lot of the fixtures we had lacked dimming controls. We also dealt with a lot of user error, with professors here at San Jac leaving lights on or off. Most of the fixtures were older models that needed to be upgraded to LED to improve energy efficiency and curb that user error. That is why we brought E3 in to rectify those issues. The most significant improvement we have seen has been in building C11 and the library. The occupancy sensors are the golden ticket; they ensure that when no one is in a room, the lights remain off, but as soon as a professor walks in, they turn on, which also enhances safety. E3 made this one of the easiest projects I have ever worked on. Much of the work was done after hours because we had classes during the day. The way I like to phrase it is like ninjas: E3 does the work and gets out, and when managers come in the next day, the work is complete but it seems like no one was ever there. The project was completed quickly, within budget, and across all three buildings, I have heard zero complaints. If you want a company that not only pays attention to the technical scope of the work but is also personal enough to care about you and what you bring to the table, E3 is phenomenal. I would recommend them a thousand times over. We have more projects coming up, and because I love the quality of their work, I will constantly return to E3.

video: Shannon Trejo, Deputy Commissioner of Schools Programs, Texas Education Agency
cleaned_text: One of the greatest benefits of working with Texas A&M University-Commerce in their doctoral program was being able to enroll in an online program that provided the flexibility to set my own hours. I could schedule study time and flex it in any way I needed. I had constant support from my professors, who were willing to meet with me in person, via Zoom, by phone, or email—they were super responsive. Finding a passion for my dissertation allowed me to focus on what I really wanted, which was for kids to be able to read. I knew I would be super passionate about this topic and wanted to learn more about reading academies. I connected this research to the work we were doing in my school district, and it organically found its way to a conclusion where I was able to utilize that data to make meaningful changes in our district.

video: Stockdale Lagoon Restoration: A Cost-Effective Alternative to Mechanical Dredging
cleaned_text: My name is Stephen Mayfield, and I am the city manager for the city of Stockdale, Texas. Originally, we were looking at our lagoon system. We had a large amount of accumulated sludge from years of piecemeal neglect. There were actually large areas that had no freeboard left. The project has made a huge difference on the first pond, where the largest portion of the sludge was. You can see a night-and-day difference; before, there was no water there at all, just sludge. We have new development coming into town, and for that to happen, we must restore the reserve capacity in our wastewater treatment plant. Most small cities do not have the money to spend on dredging. E3 is who put us together with Nano Gas. Working with them has been a great experience. They are highly professional, and they always come up with the right solution to the problem.

video: TASB approval.mp4
cleaned_text: TASB represents all the school districts in the state of Texas, and they are not going to endorse a company they cannot trust. I think that backing is an extra benefit that makes everyone feel comfortable hiring E3.

video: The Caldwell ISD Safety Team, winner of the 2024 TASBO Pathfinder Award
cleaned_text: The Caldwell ISD safety team collaborated with safety committees and law enforcement to design a safety plan, which led to valuable feedback and a more comprehensive strategy for keeping students safe during emergencies. Being a small town, we gathered input from teachers, law enforcement, our SROs, and the fire department. It is that small-town collaboration of everyone working together that creates a safe environment for our kids. I want everyone to know that every decision we make and every penny we spend is with students in mind. It is the decisions behind the scenes, the 24-hour communication, the phone calls from parents or staff, and the weekend facilities maintenance that happens when no one is around, that ensure our doors are locked and our children remain safe.

video: The Caldwell ISD Safety Team, winner of the 2024 TASBO Pathfinder Award
cleaned_text: Our kids are safe. If something does happen, our students and staff are prepared. We focus on making sure all of those safety protocols fall into place because we truly love our kids.

video: When the lights where turn on lights, people were in awe
cleaned_text: We had a very antiquated auditorium where the lights had not worked consistently for about 20 years, with maybe a third of the bulbs constantly out. We replaced everything with all-new LED house lights and ceiling fixtures. When we turned them on, people were in awe. Our school colors are orange and white, and when the new LED lights came on, you could see that our seats were actually bright orange. Every single bulb worked, and that was a huge milestone. E3 made it all work, and it is now a beautiful auditorium.

video: Working with E3 is simple, least stressful project
cleaned_text: The construction process with E3 was simple. It was one of the least stressful projects I have ever managed in terms of monitoring the general contractor and subcontractors. Everything was scheduled after hours, on weekends, or during holidays, completely working around school hours so there was never any impact on the school day or instructional learning. Teachers would leave in the afternoon and return the next day to find their classrooms fully converted to LED lighting, with no idea the work had even occurred until they turned on the lights the next morning. It was very seamless and easy to work with their construction crew. They were highly responsive to phone calls at any time of day; even after working all night, they would answer calls early the next morning and immediately jump on anything we needed resolved.

video: Client Testimonial
cleaned_text: This was probably the best-run project that I have ever been a part of.
